UMSF Incident Lab¶

Evidence-aware multisensor monitoring · Standalone Colab edition 1.2.0¶

An executable research narrative with embedded code, data and verification.

This notebook turns the supplied UMSF dataset package into an end-to-end analytical laboratory: load → validate → reproduce → visualize → explore → export. Use Runtime → Run all on a CPU. The notebook itself is sufficient; do not upload a separate dataset or mount Drive.

Self-sufficient cells. Section 1 writes a small verified runtime (umsf_lab.py) next to the notebook. After it has run once, every analysis cell can be executed on its own, in any order, and again after Runtime → Restart session: each cell begins with from umsf_lab import *, and shared results (incident data, Study A/B, the as-of replay, checks) are computed on first use and cached.

Evidence statement. Study A/B are synthetic re-implementations constructed to reproduce supplied aggregates. Stage 1 is a bench transcription (HR is a synthetic test field); Stage 2 is a synthetic re-enactment. The incident scenario is simulated. No human-subject observations are included. Reproducing reference numbers is not independent scientific validation.

Authors (source metadata): Olga Torstensson; Dmytro Prokopovych-Tkachenko; Saltanat Adilzhanova; Mariia Tykhonenko; Gulzhanat Beketova; Madina Sydybayeva.

Reading route: 1–4 setup and evidence inventory; 5–12 detector evaluation; 13–16 ingestion and quality; 17–22 incident replay; 23–25 bench/protocol; 26–28 resources and security; 29–32 verification, interactive exploration and exports. Every figure has an interpretation.

2. Runtime record and plotting conventions¶

Teal denotes available observations, blue denotes reference/regular behavior, amber marks qualified warnings, and grey denotes missing or unknown evidence. Colors never establish a diagnosis. Figures are saved as high-resolution PNG and scalable SVG. CSV exports preserve the numerical results.

3. Architecture and the evidence boundary¶

Records take three routes after validation: accepted data, idempotent duplicate handling, or audit logs/quarantine. Roster denominators and arrival cutoffs are applied before current-state summaries. The analysis layer does not command equipment or dispatch responders.

Interpretation. Quarantine is an explicit outcome. Only accepted evidence enters downstream analytical summaries.

4. Data inventory, missingness and delay¶

We inspect the incident files without filling gaps. Channel absence is part of the evidence model: for example, every incident SpO2 value is intentionally missing because no validated estimator is claimed. A valid record can contain missing channels. Stored-record delay is receipt minus measurement.

Interpretation. Record counts reflect different sampling intervals; stationary nodes are not personnel.

Interpretation. SpO2 is entirely unavailable by design. This plot excludes absent records; later availability plots expose communication gaps.

Interpretation. The long-delay tail contains buffered records. Their historical availability must not be interpreted as timely availability during the outage.

5. Study A — generate the full synthetic experiment¶

Twelve virtual workers are observed for seven eight-hour shifts at one-minute resolution. The first two days define baselines; the remaining five days are evaluated. Baseline statistics are fitted by worker and activity, keeping evaluation days out of baseline estimation.

The reference seed is 20260908. The simulation contains 10 strong episodes, five weak episodes and 10 short degraded-monitoring intervals. Model parameters were selected in the source package to reproduce manuscript aggregates; this is a designed benchmark, not an independent validation set.

[umsf_lab] Study A reference simulation prepared in 0.5 s
Phase Records Days
0 baseline 11520 2
1 evaluation 28800 5

Interpretation. Activity changes the feature distributions. Baseline normalization is worker- and activity-specific, rather than using a single population threshold.

6. Detector mechanics and an episode close-up¶

The directional scores are $z_{HR}=(HR-\mathrm{median}_{HR})/s_{HR}$ and $z_{O2}=(\mathrm{median}_{O2}-SpO2)/s_{O2}$, where $s=\max(1.4826\,MAD,\mathrm{floor})$. Both scores must exceed 3 for three consecutive eligible minutes. Eligibility requires available channels and quality ≥ 0.8. A group event then requires $n\geq5$, $n/N\geq0.70$, $m\geq3$ and $m/n\geq0.50$. These thresholds describe software behavior; they are not medical thresholds.

Interpretation. The shaded interval is injected ground truth. The three-minute persistence rule creates a two-minute confirmation delay at the start of a strong episode.

7. Full evaluation timeline¶

The heatmaps use one row per zone-shift and one column per minute. Ground truth and algorithm output are separate layers. Grey means insufficient monitoring evidence, which must not be read as normal.

Interpretation. Strong episodes are detected after persistence confirmation; weak episodes are missed at the reference threshold. Grey intervals represent observation limitations.

8. Performance: units and denominators¶

Here the evaluation unit is a zone-minute. Precision $=TP/(TP+FP)$, recall $=TP/(TP+FN)$, and $F_1=2TP/(2TP+FP+FN)$. Episode detection is a separate metric.

The inherited binary evaluator treats insufficient-evidence minutes as non-alerts. We reproduce that definition but also report availability and specificity restricted to eligible background minutes. This prevents the 50 degraded intervals from silently becoming reassuring observations.

Interpretation. High precision coexists with missed weak episodes. These numbers characterize the configured synthetic generator only.

Monitoring availability Eligible background zone-minutes Eligible-only specificity Insufficient-evidence zone-minutes
0 0.989583 4350 1.0 50

Interpretation. 100 missed zone-minutes belong to weak episodes; another 20 arise from persistence delay. Episode counts and zone-minute counts must not be interchanged.

12. Monitoring coverage and the group rule¶

The grid below evaluates the deterministic eligibility rule over feasible worker counts. The roster is fixed at six. Increasing the number of flags cannot compensate for insufficient coverage: grey cells have too few eligible workers to support a group decision.

Interpretation. Cells with m > n are impossible and omitted. Codes 0/1/2 describe evidence states, not a measure of event severity.

13. Study B — ingestion, deduplication and quarantine¶

We regenerate the challenge stream and run the original storage/export pipeline. The accounting is 2,173 input lines = 2,160 first identities + six duplicates + one conflicting redelivery + six invalid lines. The conflicting identity is then withheld in full, leaving 2,159 exportable records.

[umsf_lab] Study B ingestion run prepared in 0.8 s
input_lines unique_identities duplicates conflicts rejected exported summaries windows_per_site expected_per_window fresh_expected fresh_good_range min_fresh_devices_good selfchecks_passed selfchecks_failed manifest_exports
0 2173 2160 6 1 6 2159 12 {'SITE-A': 6, 'SITE-B': 6} [180] [36] [33, 36] 6 10 0 6

Interpretation. The conflict is one extra input line and causes one complete identity to be quarantined. It is not an additional independent observation.

14. Delay and quality are distinct dimensions¶

The generated Study B base records have separate quality degradation and arrival-delay injections. A record can be syntactically valid yet poor quality or late. The plots use base records, including the identity later quarantined, so their denominator is 2,160 rather than the 2,159 exported records.

Interpretation. Quality gating and timeliness gating solve different problems; a complete transport record is not necessarily usable current evidence.

15. Coverage, completeness and freshness¶

For six rostered devices, the five-minute denominator is $6\times300/10=180$ and the last-minute denominator is $6\times60/10=36$. Device coverage asks how many devices reported; sample completeness asks how many expected records arrived by cutoff. We display both rather than collapsing them into one score. A 100% device-coverage value does not imply a complete stream.

Interpretation. All devices can report while some samples remain late, missing or poor quality. Fresh-good fraction uses 36 expected last-minute samples.

Interpretation. Later-arriving records belong to history. Their eventual presence does not improve the original on-time completeness value.

17. Incident replay — evidence available at each cutoff¶

We replay the original state functions at 30-second intervals. Receipt/report times are respected, so future arrivals cannot leak into earlier states. Personnel states are fresh, stale or missing; stationary states are current, stale or unknown. These are evidence states, not health or structural classifications. Both event and record streams are synthetic.

Optimization note. Before each call, the runtime keeps only the latest measured-and-received record per device – exactly the record the original functions select – so timestamps are not re-parsed 122 times. A built-in guard compares this with unfiltered calls of the original functions.

[umsf_lab] Incident as-of replay prepared in 1.1 s

Interpretation. Initial missing/unknown states reflect receipt delays. A link-loss event forces unknown evidence; it does not establish physical destruction or a casualty.

18. Station channels around the simulated incident¶

Six channels are displayed on their own physical or instrument scale. Every node is reindexed onto the expected one-second grid, leaving gaps as missing values. This is a retrospective view of stored records. MQ-2 voltage and sound index are instrument outputs, not gas concentration or acoustic dose.

Interpretation. Unverified mounting and uncalibrated channels limit interpretation. The dashed line is the injected event time, not an independently inferred strike.

19. Event timeline and provenance¶

Events are grouped by their declared source class. The synthetic authoritative external report is kept distinct from local impact cues. The dataset's simulated operator association links provenance chains without upgrading the local composite into an independent attribution.

Interpretation. Timeline placement uses observation times. The as-of replay separately uses report times, preserving what was actually available at each cutoff.

Interpretation. Source classes constrain interpretation. An external strike report in this scenario is a simulated feed record, not a real-world incident claim.

20. Availability without interpolation¶

This plot counts stored physiological records per expected device-minute. Six samples are expected per minute; zero means no stored records in that bucket, not a zero physiological measurement. The second plot shows delayed arrivals explicitly for the device that buffers during a link outage.

Interpretation. Record-count zero represents absent observations. Points above the diagonal arrived later; connecting physiological values across that gap would hide the evidence loss.

25. Protocol round trips, fragmentation and CRC¶

We decode all supplied binary station frames, then fragment and reassemble one at a small payload size. A controlled one-bit corruption is detected in a compact packet. CRC protects against accidental corruption; it is not a cryptographic authentication mechanism.

[umsf_lab] Protocol checks prepared in 0.0 s
decoded_frames all_crc_valid reassembly_exact compact_bytes corruption_detected
0 179 True True 20 True

Interpretation. Reassembly is exact even when fragments arrive in reverse order in this test. Physical BLE transport is not exercised by the notebook.

26. Capacity-constrained service allocation¶

The original four-service example maximizes $\sum_i w_i y_i$ with binary $y_i$, capacity $\sum_i d_i y_i\le B$, mandatory services and prerequisites. The normalized score is $Q=100\sum_i w_i y_i/\sum_i w_i$. Exhaustive enumeration is practical for four services.

This is an abstract capacity example. It does not ingest the incident's asset-status reports or dispatch teams. Infeasible capacity stays undefined, rather than being assigned a misleading zero score.

Interpretation. The stepwise frontier results from indivisible services. Mandatory communications and lighting require at least three units before any solution is feasible.

27. Storage sizing and sampling trade-offs¶

The analytical allowance uses 1,500 bytes per record and decimal MB. At 12 nodes and a ten-second interval, the eight-hour total is 51.84 MB. The model excludes indexes, filesystem overhead, backups, protocol overhead and compression; it is not measured storage or throughput.

Interpretation. Smaller sampling intervals increase the modeled data volume linearly. The assumed bytes per record should be replaced with measured values for an actual deployment.

28. Host-side cryptographic demonstration¶

The original demonstration verifies 40,320 protected synthetic records and challenges four negative classes with 1,000 cases each: ciphertext alteration, signature mismatch, replay and stale delivery. Demo keys and nonce state are for reproducibility; this does not test production enrollment, hardware transport, key custody or distributed clock security.

[umsf_lab] Cryptographic demonstration prepared in 10.5 s
Class Cases Rejected

Interpretation. All configured negative cases are rejected in this host-side demo. The finite challenge set does not prove comprehensive system security.

30. What this notebook establishes — and what remains open¶

Established by this run Not established
Embedded payload and retained source/data hashes match Authenticity of external manuscript claims
Original unit tests and reference comparisons pass Physical BLE/MQTT/serial reliability
Synthetic missingness, cutoffs and quarantine behave as specified Clinical, structural or gas-measurement validity
Configured cryptographic challenges are rejected Operational key management or complete security
Capacity example and storage formulas reproduce A validated incident response or restoration plan

The most important analytical distinction is between a non-alert with sufficient evidence and an inability to observe. Keep that distinction in figures, exports and manuscripts. The synthetic data are appropriate for software demonstrations and reproducibility exercises, with their origin made explicit. Any empirical evaluation requires separately obtained and documented observations.
